Day 1
From Hotel: 30 min → Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall
1. Ananta Samakhom Throne Hall
A royal reception hall in Dusit Palace commissioned by King Chulalongkorn and completed in 1915. The Italian Renaissance building — clad in Carrara marble with a central dome — was designed by Annibale Rigotti and Mario Tamagno. The interior is open as a museum of Thai arts and crafts.

Dusit Palace · Dusit
9 min · 2 min → Vimanmek Mansion
2. Vimanmek Mansion
The world's largest golden teak wood building, constructed 1900–1901 as a royal residence for King Rama V within the Dusit Palace complex. Now a museum displaying royal household artefacts, personal effects, and early 20th-century furnishings from the reign of Rama V.

18 min · 7 min → Wat Benchamabophit
3. Wat Benchamabophit
The Marble Temple — completed in 1911 under King Chulalongkorn, built entirely of Carrara marble imported from Italy. The cloisters hold 52 Buddha statues representing every mudra and regional style found across Asia. The temple appears on the reverse of the five-baht coin.
Read more

21 min → Royal Barge National Museum
4. Royal Barge National Museum
A dry-dock warehouse on a Thonburi canal housing the royal ceremonial barge fleet. The centrepiece is the Suphannahong — a 46-metre golden swan barge carved from a single teak tree, crewed by 50 oarsmen in full regalia during the Royal Barge Procession. Last deployed in 2019 for the royal coronation.

Day 2
From Hotel: 14 min · 14 min → King Power MahaNakhon SkyWalk
1. King Power MahaNakhon SkyWalk
Bangkok's highest observation point at 314 m, perched atop the nation's tallest skyscraper. A glass-floored skydeck looks straight down 78 floors to street level. Inside, the SkyVerse immersive experience recreates Bangkok's history through room-scale projections from the capital's founding to its future.

21 min · 18 min → Lumphini Park
2. Lumphini Park
A 57.6-hectare public park in central Bangkok, opened in 1925 as Thailand's first public park. The grounds contain an artificial lake for paddle boats, tree-lined paths, and an outdoor gym. Monitor lizards — up to 2 metres long — inhabit the lake margins and are regularly visible from the pathways.

29 min → Wat Yannawa
3. Wat Yannawa
A temple on Charoen Krung Road built by King Rama III in the 1840s in the form of a 40-metre Chinese junk — the only temple in the world built to replicate a sailing ship. The hull contains two chedis serving as masts, built to preserve the memory of the junks that once crowded the Chao Phraya.

4. Bangkok Reflection
A multi-floor rooftop experience on the 58th–61st floors of One City Centre, combining an open-air observation deck with large-format digital art. The centrepiece is the Akara Sky Hanuman — a colossal illuminated guardian deity visible from across Ploenchit. Views sweep over Lumpini Park and the central skyline.

Day 3
From Hotel: 35 min → Grand Palace
1. Grand Palace
The ceremonial heart of the Thai kingdom, built in 1782 as the seat of the Chakri dynasty. The walled compound covers 218,000 sq m and holds Wat Phra Kaew — home of the sacred Emerald Buddha — alongside the Grand Throne Hall and the Royal Reception Halls used for coronations and state ceremonies.
Read more

13 min · 6 min → Wat Pho
2. Wat Pho
A royal temple complex on Rattanakosin Island dating from the 16th century, expanded by King Rama I in 1788. The complex houses a 46-metre-long Reclining Buddha covered in gold leaf, and is recognised as the birthplace of traditional Thai massage — massage pavilions operate within the grounds.
Read more

~1 hr 30 min
2 Sanam Chai Road · Phra Nakhon
6 min · 20 min → Wat Arun
3. Wat Arun
The Temple of Dawn occupies the west bank of the Chao Phraya, reached by a short cross-river ferry from Tha Tien Pier. Its 70-metre central prang is decorated with Chinese porcelain fragments and seashells set into plaster — work carried out during the reign of King Rama II in the early 19th century.
Read more

24 min · 19 min → National Museum Bangkok
4. National Museum Bangkok
The largest museum in Southeast Asia, in an 18th-century palace complex. The collection spans 5,000 years of Thai civilisation — from Dvaravati stone reliefs and Khmer bronzes to gold regalia, royal funeral chariots, and the finest Sukhothai-era Buddhas anywhere.

Day 4
From Hotel: 31 min → Erawan Shrine
1. Erawan Shrine
A public Brahmin shrine at the Ratchaprasong intersection housing a gold statue of Phra Phrom, the Thai representation of the Hindu deity Brahma. Built in 1956 after construction accidents at an adjacent hotel prompted spiritual intervention. Devotees commission resident classical dancers to perform as offerings.

8 min · 18 min → Jim Thompson House
3. Jim Thompson House
Six traditional Thai teak houses assembled by American silk entrepreneur Jim Thompson, who revived the Thai silk trade before mysteriously vanishing in 1967. The interiors preserve his personal collection — Burmese woodcarvings, Ayutthaya-era Buddhas, Chinese porcelain — arranged exactly as he left them.

4. Benjakitti Forest Park
A 130-hectare urban forest on the former Thailand Tobacco Monopoly grounds. Elevated boardwalks wind through mangrove-style wetlands while the city skyline rises in every direction. The park links to Benjakitti City Park lake and Khlong Toei MRT — Bangkok's most ambitious green corridor.

Day 5
From Hotel: 25 min → Wat Suthat & Giant Swing
1. Wat Suthat & Giant Swing
A first-class royal temple completed in 1847, containing the 8-metre-tall Phra Si Sakayamuni Buddha — one of the largest bronze Buddha images in Thailand. Directly in front stands the 21-metre-tall red teak Giant Swing, erected in 1784 and used in Brahmin ceremonies until 1935.

2. Wat Ratchanatdaram Worawihan · Loha Prasat
A royal temple built in 1846 under King Rama III, housing the Loha Prasat — an iron-spired multi-tiered tower with 37 metal spires representing the 37 virtues of enlightenment. One of only three Loha Prasat temples ever built in the world, the others being in India and Sri Lanka.

3. Wat Traimit
Home to the world's largest solid gold Buddha — a 3-metre seated image weighing 5.5 tonnes. Discovered in 1955 when a plaster coating cracked during a move, revealing the gold beneath; hidden for centuries to protect it from the Burmese. The marble building housing it stands 16 storeys high.

1. Wat Mahathat
A 14th-century royal temple that was the seat of the supreme patriarch of Ayutthaya. Its ruins contain the image synonymous with the city: a stone Buddha head entwined in the roots of a banyan tree, created when the tree slowly grew around a dislodged head after Burmese forces sacked Ayutthaya in 1767.
Read more

15 min · 4 min → Wat Phra Si Sanphet
2. Wat Phra Si Sanphet
The grandest temple of the Ayutthaya royal palace, used for royal cremation ceremonies and holding the ashes of three kings. Once housing a 16-metre Buddha clad in 173 kg of gold — melted down by Burmese invaders in 1767 — now defined by three restored bell-shaped chedis, the defining image of ancient Ayutthaya.
Read more

11 min → Wat Chaiwatthanaram
3. Wat Chaiwatthanaram
A 17th-century royal temple on the Chao Phraya's west bank. Its design mirrors Khmer cosmology: a central 35-metre prang representing Mount Meru, ringed by four corner prangs and a gallery of 120 headless seated Buddhas. The silhouette reflected in the river is the signature vista of Ayutthaya.

Local Tastes
Pad Thai
Stir-fried rice noodles with egg, bean sprouts, and dried shrimp, tossed in a tamarind-fish sauce glaze and finished with peanuts and fresh lime. Bangkok's most famous street dish, refined to an art form at old riverside noodle stalls.
Thip Samai · Pad Thai Fawng
Tom Yum Goong
Bangkok's signature hot-and-sour prawn soup — a powerful broth of lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaf, chilli, and fish sauce. Invented in the Chao Phraya basin and still best eaten along the riverside.
Tom Yum Kung Noodle · Baan Ying
Mango Sticky Rice
Glutinous rice steamed in sweetened coconut milk, served warm alongside slices of ripe Nam Dok Mai mango with a drizzle of salted coconut cream. The perfect Bangkok dessert, seasonal but found year-round at dedicated stalls.
Mae Varee · Srinagarindra Train Night Market
Boat Noodles
Intensely dark, thin broth enriched with pork blood, herbs, and crispy garlic — ladled in small bowls to be eaten by the dozen. A holdover from when vendors paddled through Bangkok's canals selling food from boats.
Victory Monument Boat Noodle Alley
Khao Man Gai
Poached chicken sliced over rice cooked in the same broth, served with a bowl of clear soup and a fermented soybean dipping sauce. Bangkok's quintessential everyday meal — morning or midnight, the best spots are always packed.
Pratunam Market stalls · Kaiton Pratunam
Food Delivery
GrabFood
Foreign number: accepted. — the same Grab account as the ride app, so there is no second sign-up or code.
Grab is the default in Thailand and the listings run well past the mall chains into street-food stalls and single-shop kitchens. The app is fully in English and takes a foreign card; hotel orders are usually handed over in the lobby rather than brought to the room.
food.grab.com/th/en
foodpanda
Foreign number: not accepted. — registration is tied to a local number.
The main alternative to GrabFood in Thailand and often cheaper on the delivery fee, but the listings lean towards chains and the app pushes its own subscription hard. Because sign-up needs a Thai number it is realistic only if you pick up a local SIM.
foodpanda.co.th
Getting Around
Grab
Foreign number: accepted. — register with your home number and verify by SMS; a local SIM speeds the OTP up.
The only ride app that matters in Bangkok: metered taxis routinely refuse the meter for visitors, while Grab settles the fare in baht before you get in. It takes a foreign card, and the pickup pin beats trying to name a soi in English. The motorbike option cuts through the worst of the traffic.
grab.com/th/en
Chao Phraya Express Boat
Commuter ferry along the Chao Phraya River — Nonthaburi to Sathorn Pier.
Bangkok has a ferry — operated by Chao Phraya Express Boat Co. Route: Nonthaburi → Sathorn Pier.
chaophrayaexpressboat.com.

Day Trips by Train
Kanchanaburi · 2 hr 30 min
Site of the Death Railway and Bridge over the River Kwai, built by Allied POWs under Japanese occupation. The JEATH War Museum and Commonwealth War Cemetery anchor the visit; the surrounding valley is lush and peaceful. Recommended by Fodor's, Rough Guides, and Lonely Planet.

Worth Knowing

The River That Built a Capital

Bangkok exists because of the Chao Phraya. The Chakri kings chose this bend of the river to build a new capital — defensible, connected to the Gulf of Siam, and alive with commerce. For 200 years the river was Bangkok's highway: produce floated from the north, teak came from the forests, and entire floating markets sold goods from boats.

Today the same river carries the Chao Phraya Express ferries past the spires of the Grand Palace, past Lhong 1919's restored jetty, past the glass towers of Silom. Every stop on this guide touches it. Take the boat at least once — you'll understand the city differently from the water.
